title: Spectroscopy: IR, ¹H NMR and mass spectra
note: IR finds functional groups: O–H and N–H above 3200 cm⁻¹, triple bonds near 2100 to 2260, C=O near 1700. ¹H NMR counts kinds of hydrogen; the shift (δ) shows their environment, the area shows how many, and n neighboring H's split a signal into n + 1 peaks. MS gives the molecular mass and clues from fragments and isotopes.

read.title: Three ways to see a molecule
text: Chemists rarely see molecules directly, so they read spectra. Infrared spectroscopy measures which bond vibrations absorb light. A strong band near 1715 cm⁻¹ signals a C=O; a broad band above 3200 cm⁻¹ signals an O–H; a sharp band near 2250 cm⁻¹ signals a nitrile. IR is quick for asking which functional groups are present, but it says little about how the carbons are connected.

Proton NMR fills that gap. Each set of equivalent hydrogens gives one signal. Its position, the chemical shift, reflects the electron density around it: an electronegative neighbor pulls density away, deshields the proton, and moves its signal downfield to higher δ. The area under the signal is proportional to the number of hydrogens. Splitting reveals the neighbors: a hydrogen with n equivalent neighbors appears as n + 1 lines. An ethyl group therefore shows a triplet for its CH₃ and a quartet for its CH₂.

Mass spectrometry knocks an electron off the molecule and sorts the ions by mass. The molecular ion gives the molecular mass. Fragments and isotope patterns add clues: a 3:1 pair two units apart points to chlorine, and an odd molecular mass points to nitrogen.
